paragraphs: Good first try if: you are willing to create visual works independently for long periods, can develop ideas from a commission brief and revise repeatedly, while accepting the uncertainty of works and income and being able to manage your own time and portfolio.

Think carefully: if you cannot tolerate unstable income, the lack of stable instructions, and the repetitive handling of media and tools plus exposure to chemical materials, the actual work will not match your expectations.

The core output is deliverable original visual works that meet commission or exhibition requirements, plus a complete process record: coordinated visual elements, conformity with the content requirements, on-time submission, and clear versions and ownership, not 'looks good' or 'inspired'.

Low-risk check: complete an 'understand the brief — draft — final work — revise' exercise for one small work using a fictional commission brief; it only judges work preferences, does not involve real commissions or delivery, and is not equivalent to an occupational qualification or a hiring outcome.
Decision center: whether you can make an original work deliverable under content requirements, media limitations and time budget, and clearly manage versions, ownership and delivery conditions.

Where is the boundary between fine artists and the adjacent design, visual media and craft posts?

Compare fine art, art direction, graphic design, special effects animation, craft, photography and exhibition design by actual task purpose. Adjacent posts can also create original works: art directors have custom illustration, graphic design has illustration, and photography has licensing and exhibitions; they cannot be absolutely separated by whether the work is original, nor can copyright ownership be inferred from that.
Core purpose
Create and deliver original visual works that meet commission or exhibition requirements, ensuring coordinated visual elements, conformity with content requirements, and clear versions and ownership.

Core purposes of adjacent roles: art directors coordinate visual direction and the team; graphic designers solve problems through applied design; special effects artists and animators produce visual and animation effects; craft artists make craft works with hand skills; photographers obtain images by shooting; set and exhibit designers design scenes and exhibition spaces.
Main object and basis

The ideas and visual elements of original visual works, and the content requirements of the commission or exhibition; the basis is the commission contract and work requirements, media and safety standards, and copyright agreements.

Objects and bases of adjacent roles: brand and visual direction (art directors), communication and functional requirements (graphic design), shots and animation scripts (special effects and animation), materials and hand skills (craft art), subject and lighting (photography), space and exhibition content (set and exhibition design).
Core process
Understand the requirements → organize visual elements → create by drawing or shaping → color and paint → submit for confirmation and revise → deliver and maintain.

Art direction includes budgeting and visual coordination, graphic design includes layout, images and output, animation includes two-dimensional and three-dimensional work and shot coordination, craft includes material selection, making and promotion, photography includes shooting, editing and licensing, and exhibition design includes script, space and implementation; not every special effects animation post necessarily does modeling and rigging.
Main output
Deliverable original visual works, process and version records, and a portfolio and submission materials.

Outputs of adjacent roles: visual direction and design standards (art directors), design drafts and finished products (graphic design), animation and special effects shots (special effects animation), craft works (craft art), image works (photography), exhibition and set plans (set and exhibition design).
Responsible party

Fine artists are responsible for the content expression and visual quality of the work, on-time delivery, and clear versions and ownership; the scope of authorization, payment and copyright terms are not decided by them unilaterally.

Responsible parties of adjacent roles: art directors are responsible for visual direction; graphic designers for solving design problems; special effects animation for shot effects; craft artists for craft works; photographers for images; set and exhibit designers for space and exhibition.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with clients, editors, authors and art directors according to the contract; collaborate with technical staff and production teams to implement large or three-dimensional works; when a content dispute, unclear ownership, asset licensing or a matter beyond the commission scope arises, escalate according to the contract and keep records.

Collaboration of adjacent roles: art directors with the team and clients; graphic design with business and printing; special effects animation with the technical pipeline; craft art with materials and exhibitions; photography with clients and post-production; set and exhibition design with production and venue parties.
Boundary of conclusions

Check separately by main task purpose, actual duties and jurisdiction, and note that several adjacent occupations can also make original visual works; names and task adjacency do not determine copyright ownership or authorization.

The preparation levels and employment conditions of adjacent roles do not apply to this occupation and must be checked item by item against each occupation's official materials and the rules of the unit where you work.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether the content requirements are understood properly; whether the visual elements are coordinated and serve the content; whether the media and tools are used safely and correctly; whether the work reaches deliverable quality; whether versions and asset licensing are clear; and whether content disputes or matters beyond the commission scope are escalated according to the contract.

Editorial risk reasoning: read the content theme, use and limitations of the commission or exhibition and confirm the direction of expression; starting to paint from personal preference without aligning with the requirements may cause rework or even make the work undeliverable.
Editorial risk reasoning: organize line, space, volume, color and perspective so that the work produces the intended effect; unbalanced elements may disconnect the expression from the content.

Choose tools and processes according to the characteristics of the media, and handle solvent, dust and protection requirements; using the wrong media or skipping protection causes damage and health risks.

Editorial risk reasoning: self-check completeness, detail and standards before submission and mount or organize files as required; hasty delivery may cause the work to be returned or damage professional reputation.

values: Fictional illustration commission scenario materials (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: an illustrator takes on a fictional children's book illustration commission and faces four problems. First, the text and character design provided by the client contradict each other (the text says the character is a grey cat, the design sheet shows a white rabbit); second, the reference assets include a photograph of unknown origin, and the client says 'use it however you like'; third, the client asks to increase the number of revisions from two rounds to five rounds without discussing payment; fourth, the day before the deadline it turns out that a page's main color does not match the specified color card.

Materials provided: the commission brief and content requirements; the character design sheet and the text draft; the color card and output standards; the draft revision and delivery terms; the asset source list template.

Materials not provided: who decides which side prevails when the text and the design sheet contradict each other, the licensing basis for whether an asset of unknown origin can be used, and the discretionary rules on whether added revisions cost more and on early delivery. If the exercise requires these conditions, write out your assumptions and the party to be consulted explicitly.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and communication plan, including the handling and consultation for the text and design contradiction, the handling and substitution of the asset of unknown origin, the communication and records for the out-of-scope revisions, and the checking and correction arrangement and handover items for the mismatched main color.

The plan should state which information comes from the exercise materials and which is still an assumption, and explain whether the basis is the commission brief, the color card standards or the draft terms.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the exercise)

The plan should include: content contradiction (explain the contradiction to the client and ask them to confirm which side prevails, keep the written confirmation before creating, and do not choose one side on your own), assets of unknown origin (do not use them on the basis of 'use it however you like', switch to self-made or already licensed assets and record the source and licensing, and explain the risks and alternatives to the client if necessary), out-of-scope revisions (explain that the original agreement was two rounds and the labor hours and impact of additional rounds, negotiate payment and deadlines according to the terms and keep a written adjustment, and do not undertake them for free first), mismatched main color (check the deviation against the color card, assess the correction workload and whether on-time delivery is possible, correct it after communicating with the client according to procedure, and do not conceal it at delivery), and handover (state clearly the status of the four items, the actions taken and the items still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the basis for judgment is enough.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This exercise only tests content checking, asset licensing, communication on terms and delivery awareness; it does not assess whether a real project's handling is compliant, and it does not constitute hiring, authorization or advice on real commissions or law.
Real client or unlicensed asset information must not be used; when real ownership, payment and licensing are involved, the contract and the rules of the unit where you work must be followed.

entries.question: What do fine artists actually do every day?

entries.answer: Fine artists create and deliver original visual works and carry responsibility for their content and ownership; art directors coordinate visual direction and the team; graphic designers solve communication or functional problems through applied design; special effects artists and animators produce film and animation; craft artists make craft works with hand skills; photographers obtain images by shooting; set and exhibit designers design space and exhibitions.

description.text: Fine artists (painters, sculptors and illustrators, O*NET-SOC 27-1013.00) create and deliver original visual works: this covers creating paintings and illustrations with traditional media or software, organizing visual elements, communicating content with clients, maintaining and promoting a portfolio, researching techniques and trends, drawing and coloring illustrations, mounting and framing, sculpting and shaping and installing exhibitions, submitting plans for confirmation and preparing budgets; it includes the US 2025 median annual wage of 55,490 USD (hourly wage 26.68 USD), about 26,500 people employed in 2024, a decline in the 2024—2034 employment projection (-1% or lower), the gap in mainland Chinese occupation-level wages and employment basis, and control points for media and tool safety, work ownership and commission contracts, and income fluctuation.

subject.name: Fine artists (painters, sculptors and illustrators)
subject.summary: Fine artists (painters, sculptors and illustrators) correspond in the US to O*NET-SOC 27-1013.00 (Fine Artists, Including Painters, Sculptors, and Illustrators). The core is creating and delivering checkable original visual works and making them usable: creating paintings and illustrations with pen and ink, watercolor, charcoal, oil paint or computer software, organizing visual elements such as line, space, volume, color and perspective to express ideas, emotions or atmosphere, communicating the nature and content of works with clients, editors, authors and art directors, producing and maintaining a portfolio and promoting works through brochures, email or websites, researching techniques and subject trends and shooting reference material, drawing illustrations for architectural products and models, coloring, mounting and framing, or sculpting and shaping materials into three-dimensional works and installing exhibitions, submitting works or plans for client confirmation and revising as needed, and preparing project budgets. On the Chinese side, comparable posts are mostly fine art creation, illustration and sculpture practitioners, are not one-to-one with this US occupation breakdown, and their employment and pay bases cannot be interchanged.
